opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
The two disciples were walking away, not toward anything, but away from Jerusalem, away from what they thought would be fulfillment. They had heard everything, seen everything, and now they were left trying to make sense of it. And all the while, Jesus Christ was walking with them. Speaking. Explaining. Opening the Scriptures. Their hearts burned, but still—they did not recognize Him. It wasn’t a lack of information. 
It was that recognition had not yet come.

Then they reached the table. He took the bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them. And in that moment—not in the walking, not in the explaining, but in the breaking—their eyes were opened. What had been present all along was suddenly known. Recognized. And then He was gone. Not because He left them empty, but because what they needed had already been given: sight.

“O Lord, my allotted portion and my cup.” 

In the ancient world, your “portion” meant what you were given in life—land, inheritance, security, what you could rely on. Your “cup” was what you actually experienced—what was handed to you to drink, whether good or bitter.

Because what they were searching for on that road—clarity, direction, something to hold onto—was never going to be found in circumstances lining up the way they expected. Their portion was not the outcome they had hoped for. Their cup was not the situation they would have chosen. Yet there He was, already with them, already sustaining them, even when they could not see Him.

The breaking of the bread reveals something the psalm declares: that what we are given—our portion, our cup—is not separate from Him. Even in confusion, even in walking the wrong direction, even in not recognizing, He is not absent. He is present in it. And the moment of recognition does not come from having everything resolved, but from encountering Him within what has already been given.

So what feels like a stretch of unanswered effort, or a week that slipped, or a path that doesn’t look the way it should—this is not outside of Him. This is the place where He is already walking, already speaking, already offering Himself. And when He is finally recognized, it becomes clear: nothing was wasted, nothing was separate, and what seemed like fragments of understanding were, all along, part of something whole.
